Snippet: In the knowledge-based economy, a thriving workforce is critical for an organization to acquire a competitive advantage and sustainable performance (Spreitzer et al., 2012). Considerable evidence indicates that thriving at work-defined as "the psychological state in which individuals experience both a sense of vitality and a sense of learning at work" (Spreitzer et al., 2005, p. 538)-is associated with numerous positive outcomes, such as higher job satisfaction, less burnout, lower turnover intention, and better task and creative performance (see Kleine et al., 2019, meta-analytic review). Recent studies also indicate that thriving employees are more likely to engage in takingcharge behavior, which can bring constructive change for organizations (Li et al., 2019). Besides the practical benefits, many scholars regard thriving at work as a mediator that can explain the impact of individual characteristics (e.g., Alikaj et al., 2020), leadership (e.g., Niessen et al., 2017;Xu et al., 2017;Li et al., 2019), and organizational contextual factors (e.g., Chang and Busser, 2020;Jiang et al., 2020) on favorable organizational outcomes (e.g., creativity, job satisfaction, and taking charge). For example, Hildenbrand et al.'s (2018) empirical study demonstrated that transformational leadership can decrease burnout via enhancing thriving at work. (2019) identified thriving at work outcomes, including health (e.g., burnout), attitude (e.g., job satisfaction, turnover intention), and performance (e.g., organizational citizenship behavior and creativity). Due to its influence on various employee behaviors and attitudes, thriving at work is extremely important for companies in developing talent and employee health and well-being, as well as managing competitiveness (Pfeffer, 2010;Porath et al., 2012). 

A prior study widely adopted by researchers is the socially embedded thriving model developed by Spreitzer et al. (2005). In this model, Spreitzer et al. identified two main factors of thriving at work: contextual and resources. They also added agentic behavior (task focus and exploration) to explain that individuals can be internally motivated to thrive in their work. Furthermore, they stated that thriving at work improves individual health and well-being (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Recently, two meta-analyses (i.e., Kleine et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2021) expanded Spreitzer et al.'s model by identifying the antecedents and consequences of thriving at work in a broader manner. Despite numerous studies identifying the predictors of employees' thriving at work, several concepts have not yet been identified. For example, Liu et al. In the last 2 decades, the emergent concept of thriving at work has attracted management researchers. The concept of human thriving was initially used to describe human function and how humans develop and adapt to various situations (Brown et al., 2017). More specifically, thriving refers to the "joint experience of a sense of vitality and learning" (Porath et al., 2012: p. 250) experienced by a person in an environment. Regarding the context of the work environment, Kleine et al. (2019) identified thriving at work outcomes, including health (e.g., burnout), attitude (e.g., job satisfaction, turnover intention), and performance (e.g., organizational citizenship behavior and creativity). Due to its influence on various employee behaviors and attitudes, thriving at work is extremely important for companies in developing talent and employee health and well-being, as well as managing competitiveness (Pfeffer, 2010;Porath et al., 2012). 

A prior study widely adopted by researchers is the socially embedded thriving model developed by Spreitzer et al. (2005). In this model, Spreitzer et al. identified two main factors of thriving at work: contextual and resources. They also added agentic behavior (task focus and exploration) to explain that individuals can be internally motivated to thrive in their work. Furthermore, they stated that thriving at work improves individual health and well-being (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Recently, two meta-analyses (i.e., Kleine et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2021) expanded Spreitzer et al.'s model by identifying the antecedents and consequences of thriving at work in a broader manner. Despite numerous studies identifying the predictors of employees' thriving at work, several concepts have not yet been identified. For example, Liu et al. (2021) identified five leadership models (empowering, servant, authentic, leader-member exchange (LMX), and transformational leadership) as sources of thriving and ignored the recently popular leadership model, namely leader humility.

Title: Bottom-Up Interventions Effective in Promoting Work Engagement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Background: Promoting work engagement is of interest to organizations across sectors due to the associated positive outcomes. This interest warrants research on the evidence of work engagement interventions. Intervention research increasingly advocates a bottom-up approach, highlighting the role of employees themselves. These workplace interventions often encourage employees to identify, develop, and make use of workplace resources. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to investigate the effectiveness and potential underlying mechanisms of these bottom-up, resource-developing interventions. Method: Systematic searches were conducted in the online databases Web of Science, Academic Search Complete, Business Source Ultimate, PsycInfo, PsycArticles, SCOPUS, and Google Scholar. Publication year range was 2000–2020. Eligibility criteria were defined using PICOS. To be eligible for the systematic review, the intervention study identified had to aim at promoting working individuals’ work engagement by developing workplace resources from bottom-up. Work engagement had to be measured using the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale. The systematic review included one-, two-, or multiple-armed – randomized or non-randomized – intervention studies with various study designs. Further, a meta-analysis was conducted on a sub-set of the studies included in the systematic review. To be eligible for the meta-analysis, the studies had to be two- or multiple-armed and provide the information necessary to compute effect sizes. Results: Thirty-one studies were included in the systematic review. The majority reported that overall work engagement increased as an effect of the intervention. The evidence regarding the sub-components of work engagement was scattered. Potential underlying mechanisms explored were intervention foci, approach, and format. Dimensions of satisfaction and performance were identified as secondary outcomes. Participant experiences were generally described as positive in most of the studies applying mixed methods. The meta-analysis showed a small but promising intervention effect on work engagement (24 studies, SMD: −0.22, 95% CI: −0.34 to −0.11, with I2=53%, indicating moderate inconsistency in the evidence). Conclusion: The synthesized evidence suggests that bottom-up, resource-developing interventions are effective in the promotion of work engagement. The meta-analysis suggests that focusing on strengths use or mobilizing ego resources and adopting a universal approach increase intervention effectiveness.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of when and why “thriving at work” (Tw) can fail to increase innovative work behavior (IWB), integrating empirical findings and mechanism-based explanations.

Background: What thriving is and how it usually promotes innovation
- Thriving is a self‑adaptive, growth-oriented state comprising vitality (energy and aliveness) and learning (acquiring new skills and knowledge), which energizes approach behaviors and broadens thought–action repertoires conducive to creativity and change-oriented behaviors<cite id="9939e900-1">Thriving comprises vitality and learning, with learning better predicting innovative work behavior by aiding problem recognition and idea generation; vitality contributes via intrinsic motivation</cite><cite id="9939e900-2">Vitality energizes behavior and positive mood broadens thought–action repertoires and problem-solving resources, enabling innovative behavior</cite>. 
- Empirically, Tw is positively associated with IWB and related proactive outcomes, and organizations with thriving workforces report higher innovation; Tw’s effects can be amplified by contextual resources and social ties that foster decision latitude and idea exchange<cite id="9939e900-1">Thriving at work helps employees engage in innovative work behavior; vitality relates to intrinsic motivation supporting innovation</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Thriving at work is linked to higher innovative work behavior and increased innovation; contextual features like decision-making discretion, trust, and respect promote learning and vitality through more agentic behavior</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-0">Organizational support for innovation mediates the link between thriving and innovative behavior, with a significant moderation effect (β = 0.0725, p < 0.005)</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External work contacts strengthen the indirect effect of thriving on IWB via organizational support for innovation, underscoring multilevel social-contextual contingencies</cite>.

Organizational and individual conditions under which the Tw→IWB link fails or weakens

1) Absence or mismatch of enabling resources and climate
- If core job resources (autonomy, decision latitude, information access) and relational resources (trust, supportive climate) are scarce, Tw’s energy and learning do not translate into agentic opportunity to innovate; Tw’s effect on IWB is blunted or may not materialize<cite id="cf19c44a-2">Contextual resources (decision discretion, climate of trust and respect) and process resources promote learning and vitality via more agentic behavior; without them, learning/vitality fluctuations are constrained even within days</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-2">Autonomy and social support are central job resources; autonomy lets employees use their own ideas and choose tasks, increasing application of preferences and strengths—mechanisms of thriving</cite>. 
- When organizations lack organizational support for innovation (e.g., prohibitive routines, weak sponsorship, limited budget/latitude), the Tw→IWB pathway is weakened; in one study, organizational support for innovation fully mediated the Tw→IWB link and significantly moderated its strength<cite id="c2b700c0-0">Organizational support for innovation mediated the relationship between thriving and innovative behavior, with a significant moderation effect</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External social exchanges strengthen the thriving→OSI→IWB indirect effect, showing that weak external ties can blunt innovation gains from thriving</cite>. 
- Overburdened by hindrance demands (e.g., red tape, unfairness, role overload/role ambiguity), thriving employees experience strain rather than growth; such hindrances depress thriving and shift energy into avoidant or non-creative coping, reducing IWB<cite id="6aaf2010-1">Hindrance stressors (e.g., role ambiguity, role overload, unfairness) are linked to thriving at work; these job characteristics can impede thriving’s translation into adaptive behaviors</cite>. 
- In high-stakes, control‑deprived environments (e.g., hierarchical, punitive), even high vitality can fuel “over-engagement” (workaholism), which increases ill‑being and undermines the quality and persistence of creative efforts, limiting IWB gains from Tw<cite id="cf19c44a-1">Very high work engagement can have negative consequences; over‑engagement and workaholism lead to psychological ill‑being in at‑risk settings</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Thriving employees show lower burnout and better performance, but effects depend on contextual resources; without supportive climates, thriving’s benefits can be constrained</cite>.

2) Misdirected energy and overemphasis on performance/evaluation risk
- Under performance pressure and fear of negative evaluation, surges in vitality can be channeled into effort‑regulatory behaviors (more hours, error‑avoidance) rather than idea generation; vitality’s link to intrinsic motivation becomes misaligned with extrinsic penalties for deviation, suppressing IWB<cite id="9939e900-1">Vitality contributes to innovative behavior via intrinsic motivation; when extrinsic climates dominate, this pathway can be misaligned</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-0">When employees face external pressure for creative behavior, they seek control and autonomy; without it, pressure narrows action repertoire and undermines creativity</cite>. 
- Paradoxically, high learning without decision latitude can produce “paradox strain”: employees acquire capabilities but cannot act on them; this can attenuate the expected conversion of learning into innovative behaviors<cite id="9939e900-2">Learning enables recognition of problems and confidence to change the status quo, but requires supportive climates and agency to translate into action</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-2">Autonomy regulates how emotions map to behaviors; without it, emotional resources may not regulate creativity</cite>.

3) Weak social safety nets and network insulation
- If psychological safety and inclusive leadership are absent, thriving employees may “take charge” to resist risks, yet their vitality can also heighten impatience with constraints; without safe channels for idea advocacy (e.g., sponsorship, fair evaluation), fear of negative evaluation and fear of non‑promotion can suppress IWB despite high Tw<cite id="c2b700c0-2">Psychological safety and thriving jointly link inclusive leadership to taking‑charge and innovation‑oriented behaviors; without safety, thriving may not translate into constructive innovation</cite>. 
- Sparse external networks reduce access to diverse perspectives and low‑risk arenas for experimentation; in one study, stronger external social exchanges significantly amplified the indirect effect of Tw on IWB via organizational support for innovation, implying that isolated employees experience a smaller Tw→IWB effect<cite id="c2b700c0-1">External work contacts positively moderated the thriving→OSI→IWB indirect effect, indicating that weak external ties limit innovation gains from thriving</cite>.

4) Individual-level composition and miscalibration
- Not all thriving is created equal. If vitality dominates while learning is low, energy may be invested in routine execution rather than idea generation; conversely, high learning without application can create “capability–behavior” gaps<cite id="9939e900-1">Two dimensions of thriving—learning and vitality—differ in their predictive paths to IWB; learning better predicts innovative behavior</cite>. 
- Overwork and misalignment (job tasks not aligned with employee strengths) can trigger misdirected energy: employees expend effort on the “wrong” activities (e.g., speed over quality, compliance over creativity), weakening or reversing the positive link between Tw and IWB<cite id="cf19c44a-1">Over‑engagement and workaholism can harm psychological well‑being, undermining sustained creative effort</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-2">Employees with autonomy decide what tasks to pursue and how to do them; without autonomy, energy is less likely to be misdirected productively</cite>.

5) Leadership and structure that do not amplify agency
- If leaders prioritize task compliance and do not model or enable change, thriving employees may not perceive the latitude or support to innovate; thriving’s effect on IWB depends on social‑contextual enablers and leadership practices that cultivate agency and sponsorship<cite id="c2b700c0-1">An integrative, multilevel approach shows how leadership and context turn thriving into innovative behavior by promoting decision making, idea sharing, and support</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Decision-making discretion and trust/ respect in the unit climate promote learning and vitality through more agentic behavior</cite>. 
- Conversely, if structures (e.g., rigid workflows, unclear goals) and systems (e.g., performance metrics that punish novel inputs) block agency, thriving employees’ approach energy is funneled into non‑innovative compliance, and the Tw→IWB link weakens or becomes null<cite id="6aaf2010-0">Under external pressure to be creative, autonomy helps employees regulate emotions and behavior; without autonomy and clarity, pressure narrows creativity</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-1">Role ambiguity and overload are hindrance stressors linked to thriving but impeding adaptive creativity</cite>.

Why these conditions prevent the translation from thriving to innovation: mechanism pathways
- Energy–agency–safety pathway: Vitality supplies effort and persistence, but vitality plus learning requires agency (autonomy) and safety (psychological safety) to transform ideas into behaviors; in constraining climates, vitality fuels strain and learning accumulates without application, so IWB does not rise<cite id="9939e900-2">Vitality energizes behavior and positive emotions broaden thought–action repertoires, but agency is needed to enact change</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Decision latitude and trust/ respect promote agentic behavior that converts learning and vitality into innovation</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-2">Psychological safety and thriving mediate leadership’s effect on innovation-related behaviors</cite>. 
- Misdirected energy and over‑engagement: When demands are hindrances and evaluation risks are high, approach energy is diverted to error‑avoidance; over‑engagement increases perseveration on unsuitable paths and erodes well‑being, reducing creative persistence and idea quality<cite id="6aaf2010-0">Hindrances like role ambiguity/overload impede the conversion of positive states into creativity</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-1">Very high engagement can become over‑engagement/workaholism with ill‑being, undermining sustained creative work</cite>. 
- Resource scarcity and network isolation: Without resources (time, budget, information) and weak external ties, thriving individuals cannot prototype and legitimate ideas; OSI and external exchanges act as mediators and moderators of the Tw→IWB effect, so insufficient resources and networks blunt innovation outputs<cite id="c2b700c0-0">OSI mediates thriving→IWB with a significant moderation effect</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External contacts strengthen the indirect effect via OSI, evidencing resource/network contingencies</cite>. 
- Composition mismatch: If vitality surges without sustained learning, or learning outpaces agency, the system exhibits “asymmetry of thriving,” where inputs to innovation (energy, knowledge) do not map onto outputs (idea generation/promotion) unless agency and supportive processes are in place<cite id="9939e900-1">Learning better predicts IWB than vitality; misalignment between dimensions can reduce translation to innovation</cite>. 
- Fear-based control: Under performance pressure and fear of negative evaluation, thriving employees face trade‑offs between self‑expressive innovation and anticipated sanctions; this can yield paradox strain and suppression of IWB despite high Tw<cite id="6aaf2010-0">External pressure to be creative leads employees to seek autonomy to avoid strain; without it, creativity is constrained</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-2">Leadership and safety foster taking‑charge and innovation; without them, thriving may not yield constructive innovation</cite>.

Practical conditions that increase the risk of Tw→IWB failure and how to test them
- Red flags to screen in teams/organizations:
  - Hindrance‑rich contexts (unfairness, role ambiguity, red tape) and high evaluation risk (fear of negative evaluation, fear of non‑promotion) are present<cite id="6aaf2010-1">Hindrance stressors such as role ambiguity/overload are linked to thriving but impede adaptive creativity</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-1">Over‑engagement under pressure can backfire on well‑being and creative persistence</cite>. 
  - Lack of autonomy and decision latitude, unclear goals, and rigid structures that block initiative<cite id="cf19c44a-2">Decision discretion and trust/ respect enable agentic behavior; rigid structures suppress it</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-0">Autonomy moderates how emotions relate to creativity under external pressure</cite>. 
  - Weak organizational support for innovation (no budget/latitude, punitive routines) and sparse external networks<cite id="c2b700c0-0">OSI mediates and moderates the thriving→IWB effect</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External contacts strengthen OSI pathways to IWB</cite>. 
  - Individual thriving profiles skewed to vitality without learning or learning without agency<cite id="9939e900-1">Learning better predicts IWB than vitality; both dimensions must be present and aligned</cite>.
- How to test risk: 
  - Compare Tw’s association with IWB before and after accounting for OSI, autonomy, and psychological safety; a drop indicates climate/agency mediators are necessary for the link<cite id="c2b700c0-0">OSI mediates the Tw→IWB link; effect remains significant but smaller when indirect paths are modeled</cite>. 
  - Examine interactions: does Tw’s effect on idea generation/promotion shrink when role ambiguity or evaluation pressure is high? Does autonomy amplify the Tw→IWB slope?<cite id="6aaf2010-0">Autonomy moderates the link between emotions and creativity under external pressure</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Autonomy and social support are key resources that enable thriving’s translation into innovation</cite>.

What helps the link work reliably
- Provide agency and resources: increase autonomy over methods/goals, ensure access to information and time budgets, and cultivate a climate of trust and respect; these features are repeatedly identified as antecedents of thriving that convert energy into innovation<cite id="cf19c44a-2">Unit contextual features (decision latitude, trust/respect) promote learning and vitality through agentic behavior, increasing innovation</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-2">Autonomy lets employees use their ideas and choose tasks, aligning energy with strengths and increasing creativity</cite>. 
- Build psychological safety and sponsorship: inclusive leadership, fair evaluation, and external network access create low‑risk channels for experimentation and idea promotion, strengthening the OSI pathway from thriving to IWB<cite id="c2b700c0-2">Psychological safety and thriving mediate inclusive leadership’s impact on innovative, change-oriented behaviors</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External social exchanges enhance the thriving→OSI→IWB indirect effect</cite>. 
- Calibrate thriving: encourage balanced development of vitality and learning, and align roles so that thriving employees can act on new knowledge; monitor for misdirected energy and over‑engagement that can erode well‑being and innovation quality<cite id="9939e900-1">Learning better predicts IWB than vitality; both are needed and should be strengthened in concert</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-1">Very high engagement can become over‑engagement with ill‑being, undermining sustained creative work</cite>.

Summary
- In supportive, autonomy‑granting climates with psychological safety and innovation resources, thriving reliably elevates IWB by energizing approach and broadening cognition<cite id="9939e900-1">Thriving at work helps employees engage in innovative work behavior via vitality and learning</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-2">Thriving correlates with higher innovative work behavior and increased innovation; contextual resources enable agency</cite>. 
- The link fails or weakens when enabling resources and social safety are absent, when demands are hindrances or evaluation risks are high, when vitality outstrips learning or learning lacks agency, or when networks/resources for experimentation are sparse; these conditions cause misdirected energy, strain, or “paradox strain,” preventing thriving energy from translating into innovative behaviors<cite id="6aaf2010-1">Hindrance stressors (role ambiguity/overload, unfairness) impede the conversion of thriving into creativity</cite><cite id="cf19c44a-1">Over‑engagement under pressure can backfire on well‑being and creative persistence</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-0">Organizational support for innovation mediates and moderates the thriving→IWB relationship</cite><cite id="9939e900-1">Learning better predicts IWB than vitality; composition matters</cite>. 
- Practical checks and design levers—autonomy, fair/equitable evaluation, psychological safety, innovation budgets/time, and external collaboration—protect and channel thriving into innovation; their absence is a strong predictor of Tw→IWB failure<cite id="cf19c44a-2">Autonomy and trust/respect enable agentic behavior that drives innovation</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-2">Psychological safety and thriving mediate leadership’s effect on innovative behaviors</cite><cite id="c2b700c0-1">External contacts strengthen the indirect effect via organizational support for innovation</cite>.

Open questions
- Few studies report precise interaction coefficients across settings; more field experiments that manipulate autonomy and psychological safety while measuring Tw×IWB interactions would clarify boundary conditions and quantify effect sizes in high‑risk evaluation climates<cite id="6aaf2010-0">Autonomy moderates how emotions translate into creativity under external pressure; stronger evidence across settings is needed</cite><cite id="6aaf2010-1">Hindrance stressors impede thriving-to-creativity translation but quantification across contexts is limited</cite>. 
- Longitudinal designs that separate learning vs vitality dynamics and track misdirected energy under role ambiguity could pinpoint when “thriving without agency” becomes paradox strain rather than innovation<cite id="9939e900-2">Vitality and learning have distinct, complementary pathways to innovation; longitudinal disentangling would clarify translation mechanisms</cite>.

Title: The essential impact of stress appraisals on work engagement
Snippet: Maslach and Leiter [25] conceptualised engagement as the opposite of burnout. Schaufeli et al. [26] considered it to be an independent concept, albeit negatively related to burnout, and defined it as a "work-related state of mind that is characterised by vigor, dedication, and absorption" (p.74). Vigor represents high energy, grit, and the desire to invest effort on a task. Dedication is feeling pride when faced with work challenges and absorption is being completely immersed in one's work to the point that time passes unnoticeably. Thus, the two main points separating engagement from burnout is energy and an identification with one's work. As such, organisations with engaged employees have higher shareholder returns and lower turnover and absenteeism [11]. 

In studies on engagement, researchers have been guided by the job demands-resources model [27], which holds that demands lead to burnout via a process that depletes one's energy in contrast to resources that promote engagement by triggering motivation. Despite the model's ability to predict burnout from demands, evidence for the effects of demands on engagement over the years has been ambiguous. As a result, scholars have concluded that demands alone-without considering types of demands-are problematic for predicting engagement. Crawford et al. [11] argued that such inconsistencies could be resolved if demands were differentiated into challenges/hindrances and found that the meta-analytic correlations between undifferentiated job demands and engagement improved significantly after dichotomisation. They also contended that few studies exist that measure stress appraisals as a means of predicting work-related outcomes [14]. However, neither Crawford et al. [11] nor Mazzola & Disselhorst [14] included appraisals in their meta-analyses. 

Stressors evaluated as challenges improve thriving, positive affect, and approach motivation, in addition to cognitive performance and flexibility [23]. Challenges, being more controllable than hindrances, also facilitate goal pursuit by offering opportunities to satisfy achievement needs and contribute to health and wellbeing.

Title: Job burnout and work engagement in entrepreneurs: How the psychological utility of entrepreneurship drives healthy engagement
Snippet: While job burnout has become an important topic in business research over the past decades (Cordes and Dougherty, 1993), burnout among entrepreneurs has been studied less exhaustively than in the context of other occupations (Mäkiniemi et al., 2020;Wei et al., 2015); and the limited number of studies present mixed and inconclusive evidence. In our model we define the absence of burnout (e.g., despite continuously high work engagement) as a necessary condition for psychological utility. 

Work engagement, in turn, is described as a positive, fulfilling work-focused mental state. Thus, such a focus on work engagement follows a positive psychology perspective (Sweetman and Luthans, 2010). Cardinal indicators of work engagement are high levels of vigor, dedication, and absorption (Bakker, 2011;Schaufeli et al., 2006). Vigor refers to high levels of energy and mental resilience while working, as well as the desire to invest effort in the task at hand and persist even when facing difficulties. Dedication describes a sense of high significance, challenge, inspiration, enthusiasm, and pride in one's work, which leads to a greater commitment to task performance and the overall role played in an organization. Absorption is characterized as being fully concentrated and happily engrossed in one's work; time passes quickly, and it may be difficult to disconnect from the task being performed (Schaufeli et al., 2002;Toth-Kiraly et al., 2021). Work engagement helps individuals to be goal-oriented, to focus on the task at hand, and to bring more energy and enthusiasm to the job, thereby typically enabling them to perform better and achieve higher levels of well-being compared with individuals who are less engaged (Hopstaken et al., 2015). Very high work engagement can also have negative consequences; for example, over-engagement and workaholism can lead to psychological ill-being in at-risk occupations and job settings (Sonnentag and Fritz, 2015;Toth-Kiraly et al., 2021). Therefore, the presence of healthy work engagement contributes to psychological utility in our model.

Title: Understanding the Role of Psychological Capital in Humorous Leadership-Employee Creativity Relations
Snippet: Although there are conceptual and empirical reasons to expect that an employee with high EPC will be more creative in the workplace, EPC, by definition, leaves an employee with considerable scope. As mentioned above, creative behavior in the workplace is not clearly listed as a job responsibility, and employees may even bear some risks and losses while being creative; thus, employees face external pressure when they engage in creative behavior. According to Resource Conservation Theory (Hobfoll, 1989), when individuals feel pressure, they will actively seek resources to alleviate the psychological disorder caused by stress; ways in which they may seek such resources include obtaining control and autonomy over their work. Work autonomy, as a key indicator of job characteristics, refers to the degree to which employees can independently control and decide on their working methods, work arrangements, and work standards (Breaugh, 1989). Llopis and Foss (2016) argued that employees with more job autonomy have greater freedom to decide which tasks to perform, how the work will be done and how work contingencies are to be handled. 

Employees with a high degree of autonomy in their work can decide their own work style and schedule; this can intrinsically motivate employees and meet their need for a sense of belonging. When work autonomy is improved, employees have clearer work responsibilities and obligations. All of these factors can lead to workplace creativity. Further, work autonomy can improve the internal perceptions of employees by improving their mental state and work performance (Hackman and Oldham, 1976); work autonomy may also play a role in regulating the relationship between individual emotions and behaviors (Bizzi and Soda, 2011;Wang et al., 2018). Employees with a high degree of work autonomy can participate in the decision-making process; they also have access to job-related information to the fullest extent, and are therefore less affected by contextual factors. This can accelerate the process of transformation from EPC to workplace creativity. Accordingly, we propose that: H6: Work autonomy moderates the relationship between EPC and workplace creativity.

In other words, the mediating role of psychological capital is moderated by work autonomy.

Title: Thriving at Work: How a Paradox Mindset Influences Innovative Work Behavior
Snippet: Thriving is generally considered a self-adaptive process in which employees can selfregulate themselves based on how they feel and gauge their development to improve both short-term individual functioning and long-term adaptability to their work environment (Spreitzer et al., 2005). The self-adaptive nature of thriving, which is in line with the autonomous motivation proposed in SDT, can help employees adjust to their work environment and promote personal development and growth (Wallace et al., 2016). When employees are thriving, their experience of energy and aliveness has a direct influence on organizational behaviors (Carmeli & Spreitzer, 2009). When individuals are thriving, they engage in a behavior because they enjoy it and for their personal achievement and recognition. Thriving at work closely aligns with the intrinsic motivation that drives individuals to engage in innovative behaviors (Anderson et al., 2014). 

There are three possible reasons why thriving encourages employees to engage in innovation behaviors (Carmeli & Spreitzer, 2009). First, when learning and growing at work, individuals are in a favorable condition to recognize and apply new solutions to problems. Moreover, learning enables individuals to acquire new expertise, thus facilitating the generation of new ideas and boosting confidence to change the status quo. Second, when experiencing vitality at work, individuals have more energy and motivation to perform innovative behaviors (Kark & Carmeli, 2009). Carmeli and Spreitzer (2009) argued that vitality might be regarded as an indicator of the level of intrinsic motivation, which has been shown to be an essential antecedent for innovative behavior (Anderson et al., 2014). Third, when employees are thriving, the positive mood and emotions facilitate creative thinking and enhance the cognitive abilities or skills to solve problems (Hirt, Levine, McDonald, Melton, & Martin, 1997). Fredrickson (2001) argued that positive emotions help individuals broaden their thought-action repertoires, build psychological and social resources, and contribute to behavioral tendencies. 

Therefore, we propose that employees' paradox mindset affects their innovative behaviors through thriving at work. Employees adopting a paradox mindset are led to satisfying their fundamental psychological needs for competence and autonomy, which are the nutriments of thriving at work. This self-adaptive motivated psychological state, in turn, promotes individuals' innovative work behavior.

Title: The essential impact of stress appraisals on work engagement
Snippet: Maslach and Leiter [25] conceptualised engagement as the opposite of burnout. Schaufeli et al. [26] considered it to be an independent concept, albeit negatively related to burnout, and defined it as a "work-related state of mind that is characterised by vigor, dedication, and absorption" (p.74). Vigor represents high energy, grit, and the desire to invest effort on a task. Dedication is feeling pride when faced with work challenges and absorption is being completely immersed in one's work to the point that time passes unnoticeably. Thus, the two main points separating engagement from burnout is energy and an identification with one's work. As such, organisations with engaged employees have higher shareholder returns and lower turnover and absenteeism [11].

Title: Understanding the Role of Psychological Capital in Humorous Leadership-Employee Creativity Relations
Snippet: Although there are conceptual and empirical reasons to expect that an employee with high EPC will be more creative in the workplace, EPC, by definition, leaves an employee with considerable scope. As mentioned above, creative behavior in the workplace is not clearly listed as a job responsibility, and employees may even bear some risks and losses while being creative; thus, employees face external pressure when they engage in creative behavior. According to Resource Conservation Theory (Hobfoll, 1989), when individuals feel pressure, they will actively seek resources to alleviate the psychological disorder caused by stress; ways in which they may seek such resources include obtaining control and autonomy over their work. Work autonomy, as a key indicator of job characteristics, refers to the degree to which employees can independently control and decide on their working methods, work arrangements, and work standards (Breaugh, 1989). Llopis and Foss (2016) argued that employees with more job autonomy have greater freedom to decide which tasks to perform, how the work will be done and how work contingencies are to be handled. 

Employees with a high degree of autonomy in their work can decide their own work style and schedule; this can intrinsically motivate employees and meet their need for a sense of belonging. When work autonomy is improved, employees have clearer work responsibilities and obligations. All of these factors can lead to workplace creativity. Further, work autonomy can improve the internal perceptions of employees by improving their mental state and work performance (Hackman and Oldham, 1976); work autonomy may also play a role in regulating the relationship between individual emotions and behaviors (Bizzi and Soda, 2011;Wang et al., 2018). Employees with a high degree of work autonomy can participate in the decision-making process; they also have access to job-related information to the fullest extent, and are therefore less affected by contextual factors. This can accelerate the process of transformation from EPC to workplace creativity. Accordingly, we propose that: H6: Work autonomy moderates the relationship between EPC and workplace creativity. 

Based on the discussion above, combined with hypothesis H4 and H6, we further infer that the mediating role of psychological capital between humorous leadership and employee creativity is influenced by work autonomy. In other words, the mediating role of psychological capital is moderated by work autonomy.

Title: Identifying thriving Workplaces in Hospitals: Work Characteristics and the Applicability of Character Strengths at Work
Snippet: Several models and theories of Work and Organizational Psychology contain elements which correspond to the afore mentioned concept of thriving work characteristics. Further to the previous section of this paper, the use of individual character strengths can firstly be seen as essential part of personal growth and, secondlyas described abovestrongly associated with different aspects of well-being / thriving (positive emotions, engagement, satisfaction). To reiterate and further specify the definition, thriving work characteristics should have the capacity to affect the applicability of character strengths at work. In the following, we describe which characteristics may theoretically be suited best to the concept of thriving work characteristics. 

The Job Demands-Resources model (JD-R; Bakker and Demerouti 2007) distinguishes between demands and resources at work. When employees have the possibility to use own ideas in performing the work tasks or to decide for themselves what tasks to pursue (autonomy), the probability of applying individual preferences and strengths at work strongly increases. Based on the discussion above, combined with hypothesis H4 and H6, we further infer that the mediating role of psychological capital between humorous leadership and employee creativity is influenced by work autonomy. In other words, the mediating role of psychological capital is moderated by work autonomy.

documents.title: Identifying thriving Workplaces in Hospitals: Work Characteristics and the Applicability of Character Strengths at Work
documents.snippet:
Several models and theories of Work and Organizational Psychology contain elements which correspond to the afore mentioned concept of thriving work characteristics. Further to the previous section of this paper, the use of individual character strengths can firstly be seen as essential part of personal growth and, secondlyas described abovestrongly associated with different aspects of well-being / thriving (positive emotions, engagement, satisfaction). Therefore, we argue that work characteristics that conceptually have been shown as personality-promoting work characteristics, also have the potential to foster the applicability of individual character strengths at work. To reiterate and further specify the definition, thriving work characteristics should have the capacity to affect the applicability of character strengths at work. In the following, we describe which characteristics may theoretically be suited best to the concept of thriving work characteristics. 

The Job Demands-Resources model (JD-R; Bakker and Demerouti 2007) distinguishes between demands and resources at work. Demands, as they describe them, are Bassociated with certain physiological and/or psychological costs^ (Bakker and Demerouti 2007, p. 312) and are conceptualized as potential stressors. By contrast, resources are able to increase motivation (e.g., work engagement) as they are Bfunctional in achieving work goals [,] […] stimulate personal growth, learning, and development^ (Bakker and Demerouti 2007, p. 312). Subsequently, resources may lead to better health as they can alleviate the costs of health-impairing demands. Social support and autonomy/job control have become known as two central job resources (Semmer and Udris 2004). Both include and/or promote (decision) latitudes, which enable possibilities for individually preferred behavior (like applying individual character strengths). When employees have the possibility to use own ideas in performing the work tasks or to decide for themselves what tasks to pursue (autonomy), the probability of applying individual preferences and strengths at work strongly increases. A similar effect is to be expected when employees feel safe to unfold personal preferences/strengths due to a supportive, non-condemning work environment (social support). Thus, the resources autonomy and social support comply with the concept of thriving work characteristics.
